course1-stakeholder-map-canvas-walkthrou.title: Stakeholder Map Canvas Walkthrough
course1-stakeholder-map-canvas-walkthrou.rule: Participants work on a real Problem Frame. They author their own responses before optional formative feedback. Review their reasoning and evidence without rewriting, inventing stakeholder facts, or grading. Keep their consequential judgment with them. The map will later be tested and widened in the Dojo Lab. Feedback here is a narrow check on the selected row, not that later lab. Use plain, direct language like the assignment, with at most three short sentences and one revision question. A response that meets a criterion needs no invented gap.

checkpoints.stakeholder-1: This is one row from the Stakeholder 1 of 4: Affected profile, not the whole map. Use the Field label to decide what is being reviewed. Check its answer and the Confirmed/Inferred reason. Treat inference as legitimate, never as confirmed evidence. Distinguish the person’s relationship from job title, impact from authority, and needs from proposed solutions. Questions should test experience or a tradeoff without pitching a solution. Do not demand other profile rows or all four stakeholders in this row. An inferred need is the participant's hypothesis, not necessarily the stakeholder's own wording. Do not claim the stakeholder expressed it.

checkpoints.assumption-1: This is one labeled row within an assumption block. Evaluate only that line, using its Field label. An assumption is consequential if a different answer changes the participant's next move. A question should invite a specific experience, past behavior, or concrete tradeoff. For 'What a different answer changes', a conditional next action is sufficient: changing who to talk to next, investigating a previous attempt, or delaying a proposed solution counts. The source's accepted pattern is: if a prior attempt failed, talk to the person who ran it before proposing a new fix. Recognize that reasoning as valid; do not call it merely a contingency or demand a complete two-branch decision tree. You have not received the other rows, so do not invent the underlying assumption or fault missing context. Ask a question that deepens a valid next move without rejecting it. The third block is optional.

Ask one question; do not choose a person for them or invent what that person knows.

course1-stakeholder-conversation-canvas-.title: Stakeholder Conversation Canvas Walkthrough
course1-stakeholder-conversation-canvas-.rule: Participants prepare questions for a real stakeholder, record that person’s account, and judge what the evidence changes. This is optional formative feedback on one selected report row. Use plain, direct language in at most three short sentences, with one useful revision question. Do not write the participant’s answer, invent what the stakeholder said, forecast a stakeholder response, or assign a grade. Treat a supported no-change conclusion as valid. The participant must make the final judgment.

checkpoints.validation-questions: You receive one labeled row from the validation-question table, not the whole question set. For a question row, consider whether the wording invites a specific experience, behavior, decision, or tradeoff instead of approval of a preferred solution. For a learning row, consider whether it identifies something the question could reveal about the one assumption. The separate Part 1 AI exchange checks the set; do not demand the other questions or claim to know their wording. One row may include only the selected question or learning statement.
checkpoints.first-impressions: You receive one labeled row of immediate notes, not the full conversation. Distinguish a stakeholder account from an interpretation. If the selected row is about the Problem Frame, a tentative change or tentative no-change is appropriate; for another row, do not demand a separate Problem Frame judgment. Ask for the evidence behind an impression when it is missing, but do not claim what the stakeholder confirmed or require unseen report rows.
checkpoints.report-conclusion: You receive one labeled row from the final report, not all evidence or the full Problem Frame. Use its Field label. For a revised Problem Frame, distinguish a supported change from a supported conclusion that the original frame held; ask about evidence only when this row needs it. For a move from Inferred to Confirmed, check that the participant identifies the basis for that status change. For What still needs validation, check whether the response names a specific unresolved claim and a plausible future check. Comparing named records with an account is a plausible check; do not claim a check is missing when the response names an action and source. Do not demand a schedule, completed evidence, comparison results, or stakeholder quotations in a future-validation row. Do not invent an outcome or demand unseen report rows.

course1-name-the-gap-canvas-walkthrough.title: Name the Gap Canvas Walkthrough
course1-name-the-gap-canvas-walkthrough.rule: Participants must first make their own gap list from their real Problem Frame without AI assistance. This alternative then offers optional formative critique of only the response or table row they choose. Use at most three short sentences and one useful revision question. Do not generate new gaps, rank them for the participant, rewrite their frame, invent stakeholder evidence, or assign a grade. A participant may finish without any AI feedback.

checkpoints.what-i-know: Review whether the claimed known points in this response have an observable, stakeholder, or documentary basis. You see only this response, not the full frame. Ask about the evidence or precision of a point that is actually present; do not request other points or gaps, invent evidence, or demand exactly three points if two are supported.
checkpoints.gap-inventory: This is one selected row of the four-column source grid. Check whether the unknown is specific, the 'Until I know this' line names a real decision or next step, and the blocking/useful/interesting mark fits that line. Do not evaluate unseen rows or add a gap for the participant. A useful or interesting gap is legitimate when nothing is stopped.
checkpoints.other-gaps: The participant may have more than four unknowns. Check only whether each additional entry includes a specific unknown, the decision it affects, and an honest priority mark. The source permits only Blocking, Useful, or Interesting; never suggest High, Medium, or another rating scale. Do not ask for an investigation method, which belongs in the later Learning Plan; do not demand a fixed number of gaps or create missing ones.
checkpoints.learning-order: Evaluate only the order stated in this response: check whether it includes each blocking gap mentioned here and whether the reason for the first explains how its answer could change later interpretation. Useful gaps are optional; interesting gaps should state what could make them matter. Do not ask about an unseen plan document, unseen gaps, or choose an order for the participant.
checkpoints.frame-dependencies: Check each stated planned gap against a specific part of the participant's Problem Frame and a plausible change if the answer goes the other way. The response may discuss several gaps; evaluate only what was sent. Do not invent the frame or pretend to know an unshared stakeholder account.

course1-learning-plan-and-updated-proble.title: Learning Plan and Updated Problem Frame Canvas Walkthrough
course1-learning-plan-and-updated-proble.rule: Participants develop a real plan for closing gaps in their Problem Frame. Review only the selected response or table row, with at most three short sentences and one useful revision question. They must write first and make the final judgment. Do not invent a stakeholder statement, a source, a step, a time estimate, or evidence. Do not write their answer or assign a grade. Treat a supported conclusion that another frame part does not change as valid.

checkpoints.plan-gap-1: This is one labeled row from Gap 1, not the complete plan. Use its Field label: raw Dojo material is a prior-work reminder; what to learn should be a specific unknown; why should link to a frame part; where should name a reachable person, record, system, or observation; steps should be small and ordered with rough time; how to know should name an observable result and an independent check that could show the claim is wrong. Evaluate and ask about only the selected field. Never ask how it connects to an unseen row or assume the participant has already done the learning.
checkpoints.plan-gap-2: This is one labeled row from Gap 2, not the complete plan. Use its Field label: raw Dojo material is a prior-work reminder; what to learn should be a specific unknown; why should link to a frame part; where should name a reachable person, record, system, or observation; steps should be small and ordered with rough time; how to know should name an observable result and an independent check that could show the claim is wrong. Evaluate and ask about only the selected field. Never ask how it connects to an unseen row. This gap block may be unused.
checkpoints.plan-gap-3: This is one labeled row from Gap 3, not the complete plan. Use its Field label: raw Dojo material is a prior-work reminder; what to learn should be a specific unknown; why should link to a frame part; where should name a reachable person, record, system, or observation; steps should be small and ordered with rough time; how to know should name an observable result and an independent check that could show the claim is wrong. Evaluate and ask about only the selected field. Never ask how it connects to an unseen row. This gap block may be unused.
checkpoints.additional-gap-plans: The participant may have more than three planned gaps and is writing extra six-line blocks. Check whether the supplied response carries each extra gap from an unknown through a frame reason, reachable source, ordered timed steps, and an independent way to know. Do not invent a missing gap or require an arbitrary number of gaps.
checkpoints.frame-c2: This is one labeled row from the updated seven-part Problem Frame. Review only that part. For Assumptions, check confirmed versus inferred and a gap to test any inference in this row; one stated assumption is sufficient. For What I do not know yet, check the planned gaps and interesting gaps actually stated. Other parts may appropriately stay unchanged from C1 when evidence supports them. Do not ask whether there are additional assumptions or claim to see C1 or all seven rows.
checkpoints.assumption-checks: This is one row of the source assumption table, not all assumptions. Check whether the assumption is specific, its status distinguishes evidence from inference, and the named gap could check it. A confirmed status needs a real basis, but do not invent one or demand unseen rows.
checkpoints.other-frame-changes: Review the participant's explanation of another frame correction or a justified no-change conclusion. Ask which frame part and which planning evidence supports the statement if that is unclear. Do not force a change or invent evidence.
